name: Baking soda and peroxide paste

card.summary: A home-made brushing paste of baking soda and hydrogen peroxide; each part has some evidence, the mix itself has little.
card.note: Combines a mild abrasive with an oxidiser; concentration and frequency are uncontrolled at home.

quick.overview:
This do-it-yourself paste mixes baking soda with hydrogen peroxide to brush the teeth. The idea is that the baking soda scrubs surface stain while the peroxide lightens the tooth.

Commercial toothpastes have combined the two ingredients, and Wikipedia notes that peroxide can be mixed with baking soda and salt for a home-made toothpaste. Studies of the home-mixed paste itself were not identified.
quick.mechanism: Baking soda acts as a mild abrasive and acid buffer, while hydrogen peroxide oxidises coloured pigment molecules. The combination is intended to give both stain removal and lightening.
quick.risks: Hydrogen peroxide at higher concentrations can irritate or burn mucous membranes, and whitening commonly causes tooth sensitivity. Baking soda is described as low in abrasiveness, but concentration and brushing frequency are not controlled in home mixtures.

lead: Baking soda and peroxide paste is a home-made tooth-cleaning mixture of sodium bicarbonate and hydrogen peroxide. Wikipedia notes that hydrogen peroxide can be mixed with baking soda and salt to make a homemade toothpaste [1].

Each ingredient has its own literature. Hydrogen peroxide is the most common active whitening agent in tooth whitening, and baking soda has been described as a low-abrasive stain remover [2]. Studies of the home-mixed paste were not identified in the sources reviewed.
Regulators set limits on consumer peroxide: the EU limits retail hydrogen peroxide to 0.1 percent, and the US FDA endorses gels under 6 percent hydrogen peroxide [2].
infobox: Mild abrasion plus oxidation of pigment [2]

paras: Online communities describe the paste as a cheap alternative to whitening strips. Because mixing ratios, peroxide strength and frequency vary by user, the practice is not standardised, and no preparation instructions are given here.

Peroxide whitens by free radicals that break down pigment molecules [2], while a 2017 review cited on Wikipedia describes baking soda as an effective low-abrasive stain remover [2]. Whether combining them at home gives an additive effect has not been established in the sources reviewed.

Hydrogen peroxide at 10 percent or more can damage tissue and cause burning of mucous membranes, and whitening commonly causes sensitivity [2]. Household 3 percent peroxide is noted as potentially dangerous to the eye [1]. Carbamide peroxide has been reported to increase enamel roughness and porosity [2].
